outcome: No proof, counterexample, or verified partial resolution of the square-free question for prime index has appeared in any source I could open since 26 January 2024; the question is still listed as open by the latest sources I read (PrimePages note with a February 2026 status line; Wikipedia's Wieferich prime article in 2026). The only in-window movement I found is a February 2026 status line on PrimePages claiming square-freeness for prime exponents q < 1213 (a finite check whose date of first appearance I could not establish), plus an August 2026 abc-related preprint that restates non-square-freeness in other terms and does not address the question. No AI system is named in any source I found for this problem.
problem_asks: Are all Mersenne numbers of prime index square-free? Parts: (1) the index p ranges over all primes, so the claim is universal over infinitely many p; (2) for each such p, M_p = 2^p − 1 must have no repeated prime factor, i.e. no prime q with q² dividing 2^p − 1. One prime p with q² | 2^p − 1 would answer the question negatively; a proof for every prime p would answer it positively. The statement asks for nothing else: no bound, no count, and composite indices are not asked about.

events.what_happened: Leroy J. Warren and Henry Gilbert Bray, ‘On the square-freeness of Fermat and Mersenne numbers’, Pacific Journal of Mathematics 22(3), pp. 563–564. The abstract (read on the journal's abstract page; full paper not opened) says that if some Fermat or Mersenne number is not square-free, then any prime p whose square divides it must satisfy 2^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p²); it says at present only two such primes are known and that neither divides any Fermat or Mersenne number. Pre-window.
events.delivers: Conditional reduction only. If any Mersenne number with prime index is not square-free, the square prime must be a Wieferich prime, and at the time neither of the two known Wieferich primes divides any Fermat or Mersenne number. No prime index is shown to give a square-free M_p.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The reduction is a necessary condition on any counterexample, not a verdict on any index.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for a 1967 research note
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the note; refereeing process not checked

events.direction: Cuts toward the conjecture: it constrains any counterexample tightly (a Wieferich prime square is needed) without producing one.

events.what_happened: OEIS A049094 (‘Numbers m such that 2^m − 1 is divisible by a square > 1’). A comment by Vladeta Jovovic dated 12 Apr 2002 conjectures that 2^n − 1 is square-free iff gcd(n, 2^n − 1) = 1, and notes that this would imply Mersenne numbers are square-free. A comment dated 1 Nov 2005 in the same entry says the conjecture is not true, with counterexamples n = 364 and n = 1755 (2^364 − 1 is divisible by 1093², and 2^1755 − 1 by 3511²). Pre-window. Discounted for this bullet: both counterexample indices are composite, so the prime-index case is untouched.
events.revisions: Falsifying comment added 1 Nov 2005 in the same OEIS entry; further comments 2013–2016 concern composite or Wieferich-related cases.
events.delivers: A sufficient condition for the prime-index case that was conjectured and then falsified; the falsifying examples have composite index. Establishes nothing about prime index.
events.directly_checkable: The counterexamples can be checked by computing 2^364 − 1 mod 1093² and 2^1755 − 1 mod 3511².

withdrawn.what: The conjecture is stated as false in the same OEIS comment thread (counterexamples n = 364 and n = 1755).

events.direction: Would cut toward yes for prime index if true, but is falsified; the falsification does not touch prime index.
events.object: Composite indices n = 364 and n = 1755, for which 2^n − 1 has square factors 1093² and 3511² respectively. Explicit; checked by the comment's congruences.

events.what_happened: Jacques Basaldúa's message of 16 Dec 2001 (as reported on the Prime Puzzles conjecture page) asserts that all Fermat and Mersenne numbers are square-free and links a proof at dybot.com/numbers/sqfree.htm. A reader, ‘Pavlos N’ (message 4609), replied that the formula in section 4.2 fails for p = 1093 and n = 2, and that ‘the postulate in section 4.2 is not true for any Wieferich prime’. The dybot page returned empty content when I fetched it, so I have not read the argument itself. Pre-window.
events.delivers: As claimed: every Mersenne number M_p (and every Fermat number) is square-free, which would answer the question fully. As reported by the objection on the Prime Puzzles page, the key postulate fails at least for p = 1093, n = 2. The page does not record acceptance.
events.remains: If sound, nothing. As far as the sources show, nothing is established: the argument is disputed and I could not read it.
events.doubts: (1) The Pavlos N objection on the Prime Puzzles page: the formula in section 4.2 fails for p = 1093 and n = 2, and the postulate of section 4.2 is not true for any Wieferich prime. (2) That objection identifies a failure of a step, not a full refutation, and I did not check the step myself. (3) The claimed conclusion (all Mersenne numbers square-free) is the open problem itself, and no journal publication or qualified verification of the claim was found.
events.direction: Claims a yes answer for all Mersenne and Fermat numbers; disputed and not accepted.

events.what_happened: Vladimir Shevelev, ‘Overpseudoprimes, Mersenne Numbers and Wieferich primes’, arXiv:0806.3412 (math.NT). Theorem 5: an overpseudoprime to base 2 that is not a multiple of the square of a Wieferich prime is square-free. Corollary 2: each Mersenne number M_p with p prime is either prime or an overpseudoprime to base 2. Theorem 6: for a prime q with q² | 2^p − 1, the exact power of q dividing 2^p − 1 is q^w iff q is a Wieferich prime of order w − 1. Section 3 says: ‘If the conjecture of Guy [1, p.9] about the existence of nonsquarefree Mersenne numbers is true, then we should say “yes”.’ Read from the ar5iv HTML rendering; the arXiv PDF text did not extract. Pre-window.
events.revisions: v1 20 Jun 2008; v2 23 Jun 2008; v3 25 Jun 2008; v4 27 Jun 2008; v5 2 Jul 2008; v6 8 Jul 2008; v7 19 Jul 2008; v8 1 Mar 2012; v9 15 Mar 2012 (current per arXiv listing).
events.delivers: Conditional reduction: a composite prime-index M_p is square-free unless the square of a Wieferich prime divides it (Theorem 5 with Corollary 2); Theorem 6 gives the exact exponent such a prime would have. Establishes no instance: it does not show any M_p is square-free.
events.direction: Reduces any counterexample to a square of a Wieferich prime; neither cuts the question either way.

events.what_happened: Luis H. Gallardo, ‘On special Wieferich’s primes’, arXiv:1002.3840 (math.NT), v1 only, submitted 19 Feb 2010. The abstract states there are no Wieferich primes q = 2p + 1 with p ≡ 3 (mod 4) prime. Section 1 says ‘(2p+1)² divides M_p is equivalent to o_q(2) = p’ and ‘we checked that q² never divides M_p for all Sophie Germain’ primes less that 10^11, in little computer time.’ Read from the ar5iv HTML rendering. Pre-window.
events.delivers: Computational: for every Sophie Germain prime p below 10^11, q = 2p + 1 satisfies q² ∤ M_p. Plus a theorem that no Wieferich prime has the form 2p + 1 with p ≡ 3 (mod 4). This covers the Sophie Germain family of smallest factors over a finite range: finitely many instances of a universal claim, which moves nothing on the question as asked.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the check covers finitely many exponents in one family.
events.directly_checkable: The check is q² | 2^p − 1 with q = 2p + 1, equivalent to 2^p ≡ 1 (mod q²); it can be run directly for any listed p.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; no counterexample in the range checked.

events.what_happened: François G. Dorais and Dominic Klyve, ‘A Wieferich prime search up to 6.7 × 10^15’, Journal of Integer Sequences 14 (2011), Article 11.9.2 (received 30 Jun 2011, revised 12 Sep 2011, published 16 Oct 2011). The abstract states there are no Wieferich primes p < 6.7 × 10^15 apart from 1093 and 3511. Read from the JIS abstract page. A 2007 conference abstract by the same authors describes an earlier stage; I did not open it. Pre-window.
events.revisions: Received 30 Jun 2011; revised 12 Sep 2011; published 16 Oct 2011. A 2007 conference abstract (not opened) may be an earlier written account.
events.delivers: Finite search: no Wieferich primes below 6.7 × 10^15 besides 1093 and 3511. Through the reduction in warren-bray-1967 and shevelev-2008-overpseudoprimes, this limits which primes could square-divide a prime-index Mersenne number. It does not decide whether any square occurs.

checked_by.who: Journal of Integer Sequences (refereed number-theory journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the note
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; refereeing process not checked

events.direction: Neutral to the conjecture; narrows the candidate primes for any counterexample.

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid's Wieferich and Wall–Sun–Sun prime search, started in 2020, completed in December 2022 with a search limit of 2^64. The Wikipedia Wieferich prime article says the December 2022 completion ‘definitely proved that a third Wieferich prime must exceed 2^64’. The OEIS A001220 comment by Charles R Greathouse IV (24 Sep 2024) says the search was completed to 2^64 as of December 2022. The earlier PrimeGrid run (2011–2017) was suspended for unreliability, and comments by Max Alekseyev in A001220 say its results were not double-checked. The PrimeGrid project page itself was not opened. Pre-window (the search completed before 26 Jan 2024).
events.delivers: Computational: no Wieferich prime below 2^64 besides 1093 and 3511, as reported. Bounds the candidate primes for a square factor of a prime-index Mersenne number; establishes no instance.
events.doubts: The earlier PrimeGrid run was suspended for testing unreliability, and the A001220 comments say the reported results were not double-checked. I did not find a double-check of the December 2022 run.
events.direction: Neutral to the conjecture; raises the bound any counterexample's Wieferich prime must exceed.

events.what_happened: Chris Caldwell's PrimePages note ‘All prime-squared Mersenne divisors are Wieferich’, read at t5k.org (the primes.utm.edu URL redirects there). It proves: if p and q are primes and p² | M_q, then 2^((p−1)/2) ≡ 1 (mod p²), so p is a Wieferich prime (the reduction in warren-bray-1967, restated). It says the only Wieferich primes below 2^64 (‘the search limit as of February 2026’) are 1093 and 3511, that a counterexample's p must therefore exceed 2^64 so q > 128, which it calls ‘not very helpful’, and that ‘This works for all q < 1213 (as of February 2026), so Mq is square-free for all q < 1213’, the check resting on complete factorizations of those numbers. It notes that with composite exponents every odd square n² divides infinitely many 2^m − 1. The page's only date is its February 2026 status line; I could not reach earlier revisions (Wayback fetch refused), so I cannot say whether the 1213 claim predates 26 Jan 2024.
events.revisions: Status line dated February 2026; earlier versions not reached. The page title appears in search results both as ‘All prime-squared Mersenne divisors are Wieferich’ and ‘Proof that all prime-squared Mersenne divisors are Wieferich’, so the page has been edited.
events.delivers: Finite verification: M_q is square-free for every prime q < 1213, from complete factorizations (claimed by the page; I did not check the factor tables). Per the scope rule this is more confirmed instances of a universal claim and moves nothing about all prime q. The page's own Wieferich-based argument alone gives only the constraint q > 128 on any counterexample.
events.remains: Every prime q ≥ 1213, and so all of problem_asks as a universal claim.

checked_by.who: Chris Caldwell (named author of the PrimePages note)
checked_by.qualification: Named author; the page gives no credentials, and I did not verify any
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote the note; I found no independent check of the 1213 range

events.time_since_posted: about 8 months after the February 2026 status line
events.directly_checkable: The 1213 claim can be checked by factoring M_q for each prime q < 1213 and testing for a repeated prime factor, against factor tables. I did not do this.
events.doubts: (1) The 1213 range rests on factorization data that I could not date or check. (2) Search summaries I received gave other figures (for example ‘4 × 10^12’ as a range, attributed to this page); the page text I read does not contain them, so I do not rely on them. (3) The page's Wieferich-based bound is q > 128, which the page itself calls ‘not very helpful’.
events.direction: Confirms square-freeness for every prime exponent below 1213 (claimed); no counterexample; any counterexample must have q > 128 by the page's argument. Cuts toward the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Samuel S. Wagstaff Jr., ‘Two Mersenne Prime Conjectures’, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.2. The abstract states it discusses an old and a new conjecture about Mersenne numbers, with heuristic support. The journal page I opened does not mention square-free numbers, square factors of 2^p − 1, or Wieferich primes. Discounted for this bullet: it concerns Mersenne primes (the New Mersenne conjecture and a 2025 conjecture), not square-freeness. I did not open the full text.
events.revisions: Received 1 Sep 2025; revised 27 Sep 2025 (dates from a search snippet of the same journal page, not from the page I opened).
events.delivers: Nothing on square-freeness, as far as the abstract shows. Discusses conjectures on when Mersenne numbers are prime.

events.what_happened: Vjekoslav Kovač and Florian Luca, ‘On the number of divisors of Mersenne numbers’, arXiv:2506.04883 (math.NT), first submitted 5 Jun 2025. Studies f(n) = Σ τ(2^k − 1) for k ≤ n and shows that f(2n)/f(n) is unbounded, answering a question of Erdős. I read the arXiv abstract page; no square-free or Wieferich term appears in the visible text. Discounted: it concerns divisor counts of 2^k − 1, not square-freeness.
events.revisions: v1 5 Jun 2025; a later version (v4, 3 Feb 2026) is listed in search metadata but I did not open it.
events.delivers: Nothing on square-freeness: unbounded ratios for the summatory divisor-count function of 2^k − 1.

events.what_happened: R. Laniewski, ‘Radical defects, Wieferich primes, and the abc conjecture’, arXiv:2609.00039 (math.GM), submitted 29 Aug 2026. Read from the arXiv abstract page via a fetch summary, which paraphrased the abstract. For coprime abc-type triples with a radical excess, the paper says that for the Mersenne family (1, 2^m − 1, 2^m), transgression at ε = 0 holds ‘precisely when 2^m − 1 fails to be squarefree’, on a set of exponents of density 47/210, and the defect is given by a formula involving Wieferich primes dividing 2^m − 1 and a divisor of m. It remarks that an abc counterexample along the Mersenne line would need infinitely many Wieferich primes. Discounted for this bullet: it recasts the non-square-free condition in abc terms and does not decide whether any prime-index M_p is square-free.
events.delivers: A reformulation: non-square-freeness of 2^m − 1 is equivalent to a transgression condition for the abc-type triple. It makes the square-free condition an input to the abc analysis, not a result about prime index.
events.direction: Not on this question; it is a restatement of the non-square-free condition in abc terms.

events.what_happened: A paper in the IAENG International Journal of Computer Science, volume 49 issue 3 (file IJCS_49_3_28.pdf). Title, authors and year are not confirmed: the PDF could not be opened (TLS certificate error on two attempts), and I saw only search-result excerpts. The excerpts describe an inverse-factorization method that recovers the exponent and another factor of the smallest Mersenne number with a given prime factor, used to test whether a given prime is a Wieferich prime, and frame the work around the open square-free problem. The excerpts claim no new result on square-freeness. Date unknown.
events.delivers: From excerpts only: an algorithmic tool for testing whether a prime is a Wieferich prime. No statement on square-freeness is claimed in the excerpts I saw.
events.direction: Not on this question; a computational tool.

disputes.summary: Basaldúa's 2001 claimed proof that all Fermat and Mersenne numbers are square-free is contested on the Prime Puzzles page by a reader who says the section 4.2 formula fails for p = 1093, n = 2, and that the postulate fails for Wieferich primes. The page records no resolution and I found no journal acceptance. The dybot page holding the argument was empty when fetched.

summary: Across 35 web searches and about 30 page fetches, I found no proof, counterexample, or verified partial resolution of the square-free question for prime index in any source I could open, and no source naming an AI system for it. The question is still described as open in the latest sources I read: Caldwell's PrimePages note (status line February 2026), Wikipedia's Wieferich prime article (‘A notable open problem is to determine whether or not all Mersenne numbers of prime index are square-free’), and Wikipedia's unsolved-problems list, which carries the bullet verbatim; Open Problem Garden lists it as an open conjecture (posted 2015). The substantive mathematics is a set of conditional reductions. If M_p (p prime) is not square-free, some square q² divides it, and q must be a Wieferich prime (Warren and Bray 1967; Shevelev 2008, Theorem 5; Caldwell's note). The only Wieferich primes below 2^64 are 1093 and 3511, neither dividing a prime-index Mersenne number, so a counterexample would need a Wieferich prime beyond 2^64 (Dorais–Klyve 2011; PrimeGrid's search to 2^64, completed December 2022). Finite checks agree with the conjecture: Gallardo (2010) checked q² never divides M_p for Sophie Germain p < 10^11, and Caldwell's note reports square-freeness for prime q < 1213 from complete factorizations. The only item in the window that touches this exact problem is that Feb 2026 extension to q < 1213. I cannot tell whether that claim first appeared before 26 January 2024, because earlier revisions of the page are unreachable (the Wayback fetch was refused), so its window status is open: if it is new, it confirms finitely many instances and moves nothing about the universal claim; if it is older, nothing in the window moved. Close call on the claim's status is the factorization basis: I did not check it against factor tables. Basaldúa's 2001 proof claims a full answer but is disputed and unread by me. The other in-window item, Laniewski's August 2026 abc preprint, recasts non-square-freeness as an abc transgression criterion and says nothing about prime index. Guy (1994), as quoted by the CRC Handbook entry, believes some M_p are not square-free; this is a belief, not an event. Many other items in the searches were off-target: Kovač–Luca on divisor counts, Wagstaff on Mersenne primes, 2026 Wieferich papers on prime ideals and function fields (seen only in snippets), and unrelated AI announcements about squarefree-integer problems (Erdős #848; AlphaEvolve Problem 6.52 on ab+1; a May 2026 OpenAI unit-distance announcement). None concerns Mersenne numbers of prime index.
competing_reading: One could read the Caldwell reduction plus the 2^64 search as an effective resolution: any counterexample needs a Wieferich prime beyond 2^64, which the page describes as ‘very likely’ to not exist, so the question might be counted as settled for practical purposes. That reading does not settle the question as stated, which is universal over all prime p. The opposite reading takes Guy's belief (CRC Handbook, 1994) that some M_p are not square-free, together with the observed fact that square factors of 2^n − 1 are common among composite n, as a reason to expect a counterexample. Neither reading is an event; both are heuristics.
what_would_settle_it: A negative answer needs one prime p and a Wieferich prime q with q² | 2^p − 1 (by the reduction, q = 2kp + 1 and 2^p ≡ 1 mod q²); this can be checked in seconds for any candidate. A positive answer needs a proof that no such q exists for any prime p, which is not in any source I found. For the window question, the Feb 2026 1213 claim needs (a) the dated revision history of the PrimePages note, and (b) a check of the complete factorizations of M_q for prime q < 1213 against factor tables. The IJCS inverse-factorization PDF would need to be opened to confirm it claims no square-free result.
